extracted.intended_audience: orators and writers seeking to achieve the Sublime in prose and poetry (students of rhetoric and literary style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing 'the Sublime' in literature and oratory: choice of words, figures (metaphor, periphrasis, hyperbole), arrangement, rhythm, and the balance between grandeur and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis for dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis tends much to sublimity: by expressing a thing in an expanded or roundabout way (as harmony enriches a simple air) language is made more dignified and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periphrasis to lend dignity (example: Plato calling death the 'destined journey' and burial rites 'sped on your way' by the State). Ensure periphrasis is agreeably blended and not inflated or harsh; avoid vapid or trifling periphrases that create disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of striking and appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of appropriate and striking words has a marvellous power and enthralling charm; beautiful words are the very light of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for words that invest thought with 'melody' and make facts live. But beware: imposing language is not appropriate to every occasion (a trivial subject trussed up in grand words is absurd). Match diction to subject and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plain/homely language for vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The most homely language is sometimes far more vivid than the most ornamental; familiar, common expressions can be immediately expressive and gain currency by their familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ homely phrases where they convey vividness (examples: 'taking doses of trouble', 'mincing his whole body', 'hacked to pieces'). Do not assume ornament always equals force—plain speech can be supremely effective in the right context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphors conduce to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors play an important part in impassioned and descriptive passages and contribute strongly to sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to expand and elevate thought (several vivid examples from Plato, Xenophon, Herodotus). In description and passion, a succession of metaphors can create a vivid anatomy of idea. Beware of overuse (next entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of metaphors (unless occasion demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics often prescribe not more than two, at most three, metaphors combined in the same place; excessive metaphors risk feebleness or vapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally restrain metaphor multiplicity (2–3), but allow many when an outburst of passion or torrent-like movement demands whole masses of metaphor (e.g., Demosthenes' impassioned passages). Let occasion determine scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soften harsh metaphors by hedging
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh or daring metaphors may be softened by provisional phrases such as 'so to say', 'as it were', 'if I may be permitted the expression' to forestall criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such hedges when a bold metaphor might provoke objection; they mitigate boldness and make audacious images more acceptable without losing force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion as a justification for daring language
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong feeling and impassioned movement contribute as largely to sublimity as other stylistic devices and can justify daring metaphors and numerous figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the speaker's passion carries the audience, they will be less likely to pause and criticise rhetorical excesses; allow passionate cadence to overwhelm pedantic objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole effective when natural and disguised
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole is most effective when it grows naturally out of circumstances (especially crises or frenzy) or when it appears in disguise; absurd or overstrained hyperbole spoils effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbole that plausibly arises from the scene (examples: Thucydides' descriptions of massacre, Herodotus at Thermopylae). Avoid obvious, childish exaggerations that signal the speaker is unreliable or trying to 'tamper with the facts.' In comedy, extravagant hyperboles may be credible by humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and harmony (word order, cadence) produce sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arrangement of words in a certain order—harmony of composition—has a natural power to exalt the soul; ordering and modulation of words can create majestic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully order words and reserve key phrases for impactful positions (example: Demosthenes reserving +hosper nephos+ at the end). Be mindful of metric-like cadence (dactylic measure is given as particularly noble). Small changes in word order or syllable-length can diminish the grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounding the period: organic unity of clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause derives sublimity from joint contributions of particulars; when the elements of a passage are joined into an organic, rounded period they gain power of tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose passages so their parts reinforce each other into a compact, harmonious whole—avoid disjointed lists; use the 'rounding of the period' to build momentum and stately sublimity (examples from Euripides and other poets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-rhythmical or sing-song cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: An effeminate, hurried movement in language produced by excessive rhythm (pyrrhics, trochees, etc.) degrades tone—listeners attend to the tune rather than the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotonous, dance-like regularity of rhythm that makes hearers 'beat time' with the speaker. Prevent splitting sentences into tiny, repetitive units ('hammered' cohesion) that produce coxcombry and affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cramping diction and over-compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-compression (cramping) dwarfs style and fritters away force; to cut words too short can prune away sense, though judicious compactness is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance concision and expansiveness: be direct when concise, but avoid excessive abbreviation that removes expressive power. Conversely, avoid undue prolixity (next entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-extension and prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Style becomes lifeless by over-extension—being relaxed to an unseasonable length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let sentences run unnecessarily long and loose; maintain energetic pacing so extended passages do not lose force. Seek a measured length fitting the subject and emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean, petty, or sordid expressions in lofty passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of mean or petty words into a grand subject degrades its dignity (mixing 'panniers' and 'spices' with jewels and goblets is incongruous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep trivial or sordid details from puncturing grandeur—either render such details in broad strokes or place them in appropriate lower-key passages. Only stoop to sordidness when absolutely necessary for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use descriptive series of metaphors for distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: In treating familiar topics and descriptive passages, a close and continuous series of metaphors gives distinctness and life-like picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a sequence of related metaphors to delineate complex images (examples: Xenophon's anatomical metaphors and Plato's sustained analogies). Ensure the series remains coherent and anchored in the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer loftiness and genius over faultless mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: A style that attains loftiness—even if accompanied by faults—should be preferred to a faultless but only moderately excellent style; genius may permit 'brave disorder' and occasional oversights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value grand imaginative power and sweeping excellence (examples: Homer, Demosthenes, Pindar, Sophocles) over writers who never err but never soar (examples: Apollonius, Theocritus in certain respects). Still, call on art (craft) to temper nature and reduce errors where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ art allied with nature to reduce faults
rubrics_metrics.description: While genius supplies loftiness, art (craft) provides exactness; combined they give the best results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technique and revision to correct small errors without suppressing the original grandeur—seek the balance of inspired excess and disciplined form.
